title: Hazard Perception Visual Guide
summary: How the clips are scored, what a developing hazard looks like and the clicks that score zero.

pages.heading: How the hazard perception test works

blocks.text: The second part of the theory test is a video test. You watch clips filmed from a driver's point of view and click when you see a hazard developing. The earlier you click once it starts to develop, the more points you score.

blocks.title: The rules that decide your score
items: Every clip has at least one developing hazard. One clip has two.
A developing hazard is something that would make you take action, like changing speed or direction.
You score up to 5 points for each developing hazard: the sooner you click as it develops, the higher the score.
You don't lose points for a click that turns out to be wrong.
Click continuously or in a pattern and you won't score anything.
You have to pass both parts, multiple choice and hazard perception, to pass the theory test.

labels.before: Too early: no points (but no penalty)

pages.heading: Spot it early: where developing hazards come from

blocks.text: Most hazards give you a clue before they develop. Train yourself to notice the clue, then click when it turns into something you would have to react to.

items.title: Parked cars
items.text: Clue: a car with someone inside, wheels turned or lights on. Click when it starts to pull out or a door opens.

items.title: Pedestrians near the kerb
items.text: Clue: someone looking to cross, a child near a ball, a bus stop. Click when they step towards the road.

items.title: Junctions and side roads
items.text: Clue: a vehicle waiting to emerge. Click when it starts to move out into your path.

items.title: Cyclists and motorcyclists
items.text: Clue: a rider looking over their shoulder or a parked car ahead of them. Click when they move out.

items.title: Traffic ahead
items.text: Clue: brake lights, a queue, a bus at a stop. Click when the vehicle ahead slows or pulls out.

items.title: Bends, hills and blind spots
items.text: Clue: you can't see far ahead. Click when something appears that makes you slow down.

items.title: Weather and darkness
items.text: Clue: rain, fog, low sun or night. Hazards appear later, so stay ready to click.

items.title: Horses and animals
items.text: Clue: a rider or animals near the road. Click when you need to slow down or give them room.

blocks.title: Potential vs developing
blocks.text: A parked car is a potential hazard: nothing to react to yet. It becomes a developing hazard when it starts to pull out. Clicking on the potential hazard won't cost you points, but make sure you click again as it develops.

blocks.title: Do
items: Click as soon as you see a hazard starting to develop.
If you're not sure the window has opened, click again a moment later as it develops.
Keep scanning the whole screen: mirrors, pavements, side roads and far ahead.
Treat every clip as new: one clip has two hazards to find.

blocks.title: Don't
items: Don't click continuously or in a steady rhythm: you won't score anything.
Don't wait until the hazard is right in front of you: late clicks score less or nothing.
Don't panic after a wrong click: it doesn't cost you points.
Don't rush in on the first clue: a potential hazard alone isn't the developing one.

blocks.title: Practice routine for the week before your test
items: Do a set of practice clips every day and note where you clicked late.
On lessons, describe out loud the hazards you see as you drive.
Re-read the vulnerable road users and hazard awareness maps.
Do one full practice run of both parts of the test in one sitting.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Hazard perception is a skill you build by watching clips. This guide explains the scoring and what to look for; pair it with practice clips before your test.
